welcome:
Welcome to the Analytics Team at Nkwen Traders.

I'll be honest with you: years of our sales records sit in files that nobody reads. Every week my managers make decisions by feeling: how much rice to order, which branch needs more staff, whether a bad week is bad luck or a real problem. **You are here to change that.**

You will not start as an expert. Nobody does. Every senior data scientist I have worked with started exactly where you are today: unsure, a little scared of code, and curious. What made them senior was not talent. It was **many small problems solved well, explained clearly, one week after another.**

This orientation shows you the whole road: what the job really is, how far it goes, and where this program takes you. Take your time. Then let's get to work.

day.title: Check the overnight sales
day.story: The Mobile Money sync file arrived at 3 a.m. Before anyone uses it, you count the rows, look for missing amounts and spot two branches spelled three different ways.
day.lesson: Bad data makes bad decisions. Checking first is the habit that saves reputations.

day.title: A question from Mrs. Ngum
day.story: "Did Bafoussam really sell less last week, or was it the public holiday?" You compare last week with a normal week and check whether the drop is bigger than the usual ups and downs.
day.lesson: The real job is not computing an average. It is knowing whether a difference is real or just noise.

day.title: Automate the weekly totals
day.story: Shop supervisors used to add the week's sales by hand and make mistakes. Your Python script reads every till file and produces the totals in two seconds.
day.lesson: If you do something three times, write code that does it for you.

day.title: Four branches, one picture
day.story: Sales live in one table and branch details in another. You merge them, then check the row count did not change, because a careless join can quietly double the numbers.
day.lesson: Seniors check their own work before anyone else has to.

day.title: One chart for the board
day.story: The board will not read tables. You make one clear chart that shows which branch is growing, with honest axes and a title that says the finding.
day.lesson: A chart is an argument. Make it clear, and never make it mislead.

day.title: A branch manager asks for her top products
day.story: The Mile 4 manager wants her ten best sellers this month. You write a SQL query, then add it to her dashboard so she never has to ask again.
day.lesson: The best analysts make themselves less needed for routine questions, so they have time for hard ones.

day.title: Write the 'so what'
day.story: You send Mrs. Ngum five sentences: what happened, why, how sure you are, and what she should do on Monday. She forwards it to the owner.
day.lesson: Analysis that nobody understands changes nothing. The summary is the product.

myths.claim: Data scientists spend most of their day building AI models.
myths.explain: Most of the time goes into finding data, cleaning it, understanding it and explaining results. Modelling is one step, and often a small one.

myths.claim: You need to be a maths genius to work with data.
myths.explain: You need solid basics (averages, spread, percentages, probability) used carefully and honestly. This program teaches them from the start.

myths.claim: A chart can mislead even when every number in it is correct.
myths.explain: A cut axis, a wrong chart type or a cherry-picked time period can tell a false story with true numbers. Chapter 6 teaches you to spot and avoid this.

myths.claim: With enough data, you don't need a clear question.
myths.explain: Without a question you only find noise. Every project in this track starts with a question a manager actually cares about.

myths.claim: Spreadsheets and SQL still matter in modern data jobs.
myths.explain: SQL and spreadsheets appear in a large share of data analyst job adverts. Chapter 7 gives you both, plus dashboards.

myths.claim: Senior data people mostly work alone with their computer.
myths.explain: Seniors spend a lot of their time with people: clarifying questions, reviewing others' work, and explaining results to leaders.

myths.claim: Proof of your work can matter more than a certificate.
myths.explain: Employers want to see what you can do. Your reviewed projects, public portfolio and GitHub are that proof; certificates point to it.

ladder.title: Data Rookie
ladder.does: Learning the tools: spreadsheets, first Python, basic statistics. Asking lots of questions.
ladder.trusted: Your own practice and small, guided exercises.
ladder.program: This is where Chapter 1 begins. Everyone in the track started here.

ladder.title: Junior Data Analyst
ladder.does: Cleans data, answers clear questions with SQL, Python and spreadsheets, builds charts and simple dashboards, follows a plan someone else sets.
ladder.trusted: One well-defined question at a time, with a senior reviewing the work.
ladder.program: The program's finish line. By the end you'll have reviewed projects, a portfolio, interview practice and certificates that show you can do this job.

ladder.title: Data Analyst
ladder.does: Owns the regular reports and dashboards of a team, chooses the right method without being told, spots data problems before they reach a report, presents to managers.
ladder.trusted: The numbers of a whole business area.
ladder.program: Seeds you plant now: the self-checks, the dashboards in Chapter 7 and presenting at Presentation Day.

ladder.title: Data Scientist
ladder.does: Designs experiments, builds forecasts and predictive models, uses deeper statistics, works with engineers to put models into real products.
ladder.trusted: Questions where the method itself has to be invented.
ladder.program: Built on the statistics of Chapter 3 and the habit of checking assumptions. Machine learning comes after this program.

ladder.title: Senior Data Scientist
ladder.does: Turns a vague business worry into a clear plan, decides what NOT to analyse, reviews other people's work, explains uncertainty to leaders, mentors juniors.
ladder.trusted: Decisions that cost real money, and the growth of other analysts.
ladder.program: The habits start now: explaining ideas simply (Explain it back), reviewing a partner's work, and writing a 'so what' for every analysis.

ladder.title: Lead / Principal Data Scientist
ladder.does: Sets the data strategy, builds and leads the team, chooses which problems are worth solving, and owns data ethics and quality for the company.
ladder.trusted: The direction of data work for a whole organisation.
ladder.program: Far ahead. But every lead you will ever meet once did their first data-cleaning exercise, just like Chapter 1.

ladder_note: Years are typical, not rules: they vary a lot by company and country. What moves people up is proof of skill, the trust they earn and how well they explain their work.

senior.python: Writes clean, tested code that others can still run months later, and automates every boring, repeated task.
senior.statistics: Knows when a difference is real or just noise, and always says how sure they are.
senior.pandas: Reshapes large tables quickly and checks that every join and filter kept the right rows.
senior.cleaning: Finds data problems before they reach a report, fixes the cause, and documents every change.
senior.visualization: Chooses the one chart that makes a decision obvious, and never lets a chart mislead.
senior.sql: Answers questions straight from the company database, quickly and correctly, with clear, readable queries.
senior.bi: Builds dashboards managers actually open every week, and retires the ones they don't.
senior.communication: Turns analysis into a decision: a one-page memo, a five-minute talk, a clear 'so what'.
